lead: A Fourier transform turns a time waveform into a frequency recipe: how much of each frequency the signal contains. Filters, antennas and cables act on frequency, not on time samples. A band-pass signal has all its content in a narrow band around a carrier, as in a radio station at 100 MHz or Wi-Fi at 2.4 GHz. This chapter reviews the transform and its key properties, then describes band-pass signals by an easier low-pass equivalent.
prereq: You need baseband, carrier and bandwidth from 1.1.

blocks.text: A signal x(t) is a function of time. The Fourier transform asks how much of each frequency it contains. It writes x(t) as a sum of complex exponentials e<sup>j2πft</sup>, each with complex weight X(f). The forward transform analyses; the inverse synthesises.
X(f) = ∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>∞</sup> x(t) e<sup>−j2πft</sup> dt
blocks.where: X(f) is the Fourier transform in volts per hertz (V/Hz) when x(t) is in volts; f is frequency in hertz; j = √−1; t is time in seconds.

blocks.text: x(t) = ∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>∞</sup> X(f) e<sup>j2πft</sup> df
blocks.where: x(t) is the time signal in volts; X(f) is its transform; f is frequency in hertz; the integral adds all frequency components.

blocks.text: X(f) is complex. |X(f)| is the magnitude spectrum, ∠X(f) the phase spectrum. For a voltage pulse, |X(f)| has units V/Hz: it is a density, not a voltage. Multiply by a filter width in hertz to get volts.
The transform exists for finite-energy signals and for common power signals treated with impulses.
Six properties cover most exam questions. Each pairs a time operation with a frequency operation.

items: Linearity: a x₁(t) + b x₂(t) ↔ a X₁(f) + b X₂(f). Superposition holds.
Time shift: x(t − t₀) ↔ X(f) e<sup>−j2πf t₀</sup>. Magnitude unchanged; only phase changes.

Frequency shift: x(t) e<sup>j2πf_c t</sup> ↔ X(f − f_c): a complex exponential shifts the spectrum one way, to +f_c. Multiplying by a real carrier cos(2πf_c t) = ½(e<sup>j2πf_c t</sup> + e<sup>−j2πf_c t</sup>) makes two half-size copies at ±f_c; that is modulation.
Convolution: x(t) * h(t) ↔ X(f) H(f). Time convolution becomes frequency multiplication.
Scaling: x(at) ↔ (1/|a|) X(f/a). Compressing in time spreads the spectrum in frequency.
Parseval (Rayleigh energy) theorem: total energy in time equals total energy in frequency.

blocks.text: ∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>∞</sup> |x(t)|² dt = ∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>∞</sup> |X(f)|² df
blocks.where: With x(t) in volts and f in hertz, both sides have units V²·s, energy per ohm; |X(f)|² is the energy spectral density.

blocks.text: Define sinc(u) = sin(πu)/(πu) for u ≠ 0 and sinc(0) = 1. A rectangular pulse of width T has transform A T sinc(fT).
A linear time-invariant (LTI) system is fixed by its impulse response h(t). The output is y(t) = x(t) * h(t). In frequency, this is simple multiplication.
Y(f) = X(f) H(f)
blocks.where: Y(f), X(f) and H(f) are the Fourier transforms of output, input and impulse response; H(f) is the frequency response.

blocks.text: H(f) = |H(f)| e<sup>jθ(f)</sup>. |H(f)| scales each frequency; θ(f) delays it. A system is distortionless when every frequency gets the same gain and the same time delay. In phase terms θ(f) must be a straight line through the origin, θ(f) = −2πf t_d: the phase lag in radians grows linearly with frequency, while the delay t_d stays constant.
H(f) = K e<sup>−j2πf t_d</sup>
blocks.where: K is a constant gain; t_d is the delay in seconds; θ(f) = −2πf t_d radians.

blocks.text: Phase delay is the delay of one frequency. Group delay is the delay of the envelope around that frequency.

blocks.where: τ_p is phase delay in seconds; τ_g is group delay in seconds; θ(f) is in radians; f is in hertz.

blocks.text: If θ(f) = −2πf t_d, both delays equal t_d. If θ(f) is not a straight line, frequencies arrive at different times and a pulse spreads even when |H(f)| is flat. Use radians for θ(f).

sections.h3: Band-pass signals and the low-pass equivalent

blocks.text: A band-pass signal has a spectrum zero outside a band of width B centred at +f_c and −f_c, with f_c much larger than B. A radio signal at 100 MHz with 200 kHz bandwidth is band-pass. Its positive-frequency content lies between f_c − B/2 and f_c + B/2.
Any such signal can be written in canonical form with two low-pass signals.
x(t) = x_I(t) cos(2πf_c t) − x_Q(t) sin(2πf_c t)
blocks.where: x_I(t) is the in-phase component in volts; x_Q(t) is the quadrature component in volts; f_c is the carrier in hertz; both components are low-pass with bandwidth B/2.

blocks.text: x_I is in-phase, x_Q quadrature. Both are real low-pass with bandwidth B/2 and together carry all information of x(t). The pair is the low-pass equivalent (baseband equivalent).

Why bother? Sampling a 100 MHz carrier directly needs more than 200 million samples per second. x_I needs B samples per second and x_Q needs B samples per second, so the pair needs 2B real samples per second, far below the 2f_c samples per second the carrier itself would demand. The spectrum picture is a copy of the message spectrum moved to ±f_c.
The Hilbert transform builds x_I and x_Q from x(t); that construction is in 1.3.

figure.caption: Positive-frequency magnitude spectrum of a 1 ms, 2 V rectangular pulse before and after modulation onto a 10 kHz carrier. The baseband sinc has its first null at 1 kHz, so the null-to-null bandwidth is 2 kHz. The shifted copy has the same sinc shape and width but half the height, 1 mV/Hz, because a unit-amplitude cosine splits the amplitude between +f_c and −f_c; only the +f_c copy lies inside this plot.

spec.aria: A plot of magnitude spectrum in mV/Hz against frequency in kHz, showing a sinc-shaped baseband spectrum with first null at 1 kHz and a second half-height sinc centred at 10 kHz.

examples.question: A rectangular pulse is x(t) = 2 V for |t| < 0.5 ms and x(t) = 0 elsewhere. (a) Find X(f). (b) Find X(0). (c) Find the first null and the null-to-null bandwidth. State why the 3-dB bandwidth is a different number.
steps: The pulse width is T = 1 ms = 1×10<sup>−3</sup> s. The amplitude is A = 2 V.
X(f) = ∫<sub>−T/2</sub><sup>T/2</sup> A e<sup>−j2πft</sup> dt = A T sinc(fT), with sinc(u) = sin(πu)/(πu).
The first null is at fT = 1, so f = 1/T = 1 kHz.
|X(f)| falls to 1/√2 of its peak at f = ±0.443/T, so the 3-dB bandwidth, peak to peak between these two points, is 0.886/T ≈ 0.89/T. That is different from the null-to-null 2/T.
examples.answer: X(f) = 2×10<sup>−3</sup> sinc(10<sup>3</sup> f) V/Hz, X(0) = 2×10<sup>−3</sup> V/Hz, and the null-to-null bandwidth is 2 kHz.
examples.check:
A = 2.0
T = 1e-3
X0 = A * T
f_null = 1.0 / T
bw = 2.0 / T
print(X0)
print(f_null)
print(bw)

traps: Bandwidth is not one number. Say first-null, 3-dB or null-to-null; for a rectangular pulse null-to-null is 2/T, not 1/T.

X(f) is a density in V/Hz. Multiply it by the filter width in hertz to get volts. Around f = 0 the pulse has 2 mV/Hz, so a flat 1 Hz filter passes a peak of 2 mV; a filter many times wider passes proportionally more, because the density is being added over a wider band.
A time shift multiplies X(f) by e<sup>−j2πf t₀</sup>; the magnitude |X(f)| does not change.
Use radians in delay formulas. θ(f) in degrees gives a wrong delay by a factor 180/π.
Phase delay and group delay are equal only when phase is linear; nonlinear phase distorts the envelope even if |H(f)| is flat.
Time convolution pairs with frequency multiplication, not division. Writing Y(f) = X(f)/H(f) is deconvolution, not normal transmission.

quiz.q: State the Fourier transform pair for a rectangular pulse of amplitude A and width T.
quiz.a: x(t) = A for |t| < T/2 and 0 elsewhere; X(f) = A T sinc(fT), with sinc(u) = sin(πu)/(πu) and sinc(0) = 1.

quiz.q: Why does a time shift not change the magnitude spectrum?
quiz.a: The time shift multiplies X(f) by e<sup>−j2πf t₀</sup>. This factor has magnitude 1 for every f, so |X(f)| is unchanged; only phase changes.

quiz.q: A pulse is x(t) = 4 V for |t| < 0.1 ms and 0 elsewhere. Find X(0), the first null and the null-to-null bandwidth.
quiz.a: T = 0.2 ms = 2×10<sup>−4</sup> s. X(0) = A T = 4 × 2×10<sup>−4</sup> = 8×10<sup>−4</sup> V/Hz. First null at 1/T = 5 kHz. Null-to-null bandwidth = 2/T = 10 kHz.

quiz.q: An LTI system has H(f) = 5 e<sup>−j2πf(0.2 ms)</sup>. Find the output for input x(t), and state whether the transmission is distortionless.
quiz.a: |H(f)| = 5 is flat and θ(f) = −2πf t_d with t_d = 0.2 ms. The output is y(t) = 5 x(t − 0.2 ms). The transmission is distortionless: constant gain and linear phase. Phase delay and group delay both equal 0.2 ms.

quiz.q: Write the Parseval (Rayleigh energy) theorem and give the units of each side for a voltage signal.
quiz.a: ∫ |x(t)|² dt = ∫ |X(f)|² df. With x(t) in volts and f in hertz, both sides are in V²·s, energy per ohm.

quiz.q: Why does a band-pass signal need two low-pass components x_I and x_Q instead of one?
quiz.a: A real band-pass signal has both amplitude and phase information around the carrier. One real low-pass signal cannot carry both independently. The pair x_I and x_Q gives two real functions, each of bandwidth B/2, and together they reconstruct x(t) exactly.

quiz.q: A band-pass signal has carrier f_c = 100 kHz and bandwidth B = 10 kHz. Give its band edges and the bandwidth of each low-pass equivalent component.
quiz.a: Lower edge = f_c − B/2 = 95 kHz. Upper edge = f_c + B/2 = 105 kHz. Each of x_I and x_Q has bandwidth B/2 = 5 kHz.

beyond: Not for the exam. Every software-defined radio stores signals as I and Q samples, which are x_I and x_Q sampled at a low rate; this is why a wide Wi-Fi channel can be processed after downconversion by a modest ADC. Search "complex envelope", "IQ imbalance", "group delay distortion" and "spectrum analyzer".
